newsitem.title: GERMANY: IG Metall recommends 97 pay demand of 4.5-5.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: IG Metall recommends 97 pay demand of 4.5-5.0 pct.

text.p: German engineering union IG Metall said on Tuesday it would recommend that its regional branches demand an overall wage rise of between 4.5 percent and 5.0 percent in pay talks for 1997.

IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel, presenting the pay demand, told a news conference that the union wanted to secure both jobs and incoming in the forthcoming pay talks. Zwickel was speaking after a meeting of the IG Metall board in Frankfurt.
Zwickel, who earlier this year proposed a broad "Alliance for Jobs" aimed at securing and creating employment, made clear that job preservation was a top priority for the union.

Explaining that the 4.5-5.0 percent was made up of a productivity component combined with an assumption of likely inflation, Zwickel made clear that the union was prepared to accept part of the rise in the form of job security measures.
"The productivity component of 2-1/2 to three percent, should be used exclusively for goals related to job security policies," he said.

He added that the union's aim in terms of a straight increase in the basic wage would be to ensure that pay levels are not eroded by inflation, which he noted is forecast to stick at or around the two percent level.

IG Metall some 18 months ago secured a pay deal for its members which was hailed as a huge victory for the unions, offering workers a 3.4 percent rise in May 1995 and a further 3.6 percent increase in November of that year.

But the high pay increase backfired on the union to some extent. Independent economists with hindsight blame that pay deal and others in the 1995 payround for helping to tip the German economy into a downturn late last year.
